extracted.intended_audience: readers of philosophical literature and Carlyle scholars; educated general readers interested in 19th-century social-philosophical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and characterizing the prescriptive and evaluative claims embedded in an excerpt from Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus (philosophical-literary prose about society, manners, religion, and transcendence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy as universal duty
rubrics_metrics.description: “Shall Courtesy be done only to the rich, and only by the rich? ... I discern no special connection with wealth or birth: but rather that it lies in human nature itself, and is due from all men towards all men.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courtesy/Good-breeding is a moral obligation independent of class or birth; it 'gracefully remembers the rights of others' rather than insisting on one's own. The passage presents politeness as a natural, ennobling force that should inform social conduct broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverence to the human body as temple
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is but one temple in the world,' says Novalis, 'and that temple is the Body of Man. Nothing is holier than this high Form. Bending before men is a reverence done to this Revelation in the Flesh.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bowing or showing respect to other humans is framed as reverence to the divine manifestation in human bodies; social politeness is given a spiritual justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about indiscriminate deference
rubrics_metrics.description: “...I would bow to every Man with any sort of hat, or with no hat whatever. ... And yet, alas, such indiscriminate bowing serves not. For there is a Devil dwells in man, as well as a Divinity; and too often the bow is but pocketed by the former... therefore must we withhold it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While universal politeness is an ideal, one must temper it with discernment because outward signs of respect can be exploited by vanity and hypocrisy; politeness should not facilitate deception or reward vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverence for empty/cast clothes (symbols) as purer worship
rubrics_metrics.description: “The gladder am I, on the other hand, to do reverence to those Shells and outer Husks of the Body, wherein no devilish passion any longer lodges, but only the pure emblem and effigies of Man: I mean, to Empty, or even to Cast Clothes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worshiping symbols (e.g., empty gowns, ceremonial clothes) can be morally preferable because the symbol is not alive to deceive; reverence directed at visible forms can be free of the corruptions that attach to living persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artifacts and old clothes as testimony to human life
rubrics_metrics.description: “With awe-struck heart I walk through that Monmouth Street, with its empty Suits, as through a Sanhedrim of stainless Ghosts. Silent are they, but expressive in their silence: the past witnesses and instruments of Woe and Joy..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material remnants (old clothes, discarded objects) are morally and spiritually significant: they stand as witnesses to lives, passions, and history and can provoke reflection and devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Perseverance / resistance to change
rubrics_metrics.description: “The law of Perseverance is among the deepest in man: by nature he hates change; seldom will he quit his old house till it has actually fallen about his ears.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social and ceremonial forms persist long after their original vitality has evaporated; reformers must account for this deep human resistance to change when imagining social transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical remedy: deliberate destruction for rebirth
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus is Teufelsdrockh, content that old sick Society should be deliberately burnt ... in the faith that she is a Phoenix; and that a new heaven-born young one will rise out of her ashes!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One represented voice advocates deliberate destruction of a corrupt society (Phoenix metaphor) as a path to a new, living society. The Editor's surrounding commentary adds a counter-evaluation (expectation of gratitude to benefactress rather than fatalistic trust), indicating this is a contested prescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradition/transmission: we inherit forms as well as life
rubrics_metrics.description: “how we inherit not Life only, but all the garniture and form of Life; and work, and speak, and even think and feel, as our Fathers... have given it us?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural transmission (institutions, books, language) is a primary mechanism by which thought and form persist across generations; individuals are formed by these inherited 'filaments.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Generations enable cumulative progress
rubrics_metrics.description: “Generations are as the Days of toilsome Mankind: Death and Birth are the vesper and the matin bells... What the Father has made, the Son can make and enjoy; but has also work of his own appointed him. Thus all things wax, and roll onwards; Arts, Establishments, Opinions, nothing is completed, but ever completing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History advances by generational succession: each generation inherits and extends the achievements of predecessors; progress is continuous rather than instant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero-worship as a social/psychic necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: “...there is a true religious Loyalty forever rooted in his heart; nay in all ages, even in ours, it manifests itself as a more or less orthodox Hero-worship... in which fact, that Hero-worship exists, has existed, and will forever exist, universally among Mankind, mayest thou discern the corner-stone of living rock, whereon all Polities for the remotest time may stand secure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverence for outstanding individuals (heroes, sages) is framed as foundational to social order and polity; societies need focal figures to organize reverence and loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience as precondition for freedom and rule
rubrics_metrics.description: “True is it that, in these days, man can do almost all things, only not obey. True likewise that whoso cannot obey cannot be free, still less bear rule; he that is the inferior of nothing, can be the superior of nothing, the equal of nothing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle (through the Professor) claims that the capacity to obey is essential to participate in freedom and to hold authority; unbridled individualism undermines social function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of honor derived from fighting; possible future change
rubrics_metrics.description: “Remark, not without surprise, how all high Titles of Honor come hitherto from Fighting. ... A Millennium, or reign of Peace and Wisdom... may it not be apprehended that such Fighting titles will cease to be palatable, and new and higher need to be devised?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social nomenclature reflects historical functions (e.g., military); in a peaceful era, honorifics and political vocabulary may need redesign to match new social realities. Exception noted: the title 'King' is seen as eternal for linguistic reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: New media/literature as clergy/preaching force
rubrics_metrics.description: “A Preaching Friar settles himself in every village; and builds a pulpit, which he calls Newspaper. Therefrom he preaches what most momentous doctrine is in him..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers and literature serve the social role of clergy—preaching, breaking idols, and marking sites for future religious or moral attention; modern literary forms can perform prophetic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles as confirmation of deeper laws
rubrics_metrics.description: “'But is not a real Miracle simply a violation of the Laws of Nature?' ask several. Whom I answer by this new question: What are the Laws of Nature? To me perhaps the rising of one from the dead were no violation of these Laws, but a confirmation; were some far deeper Law, now first penetrated into, and by Spiritual Force... brought to bear on us with its Material Force.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miracles should not be dismissed as mere violations; they may indicate deeper natural laws currently unknown. The proper philosophical stance is openness to deeper orders beyond received scientific law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility about scientific comprehensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: “System of Nature! To the wisest man, wide as is his vision, Nature remains of quite infinite depth, of quite infinite expansion; and all Experience thereof limits itself to some few computed centuries and measured square-miles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific knowledge is necessarily partial and local; one must be modest about claims that current science exhausts the 'Statute-Book of Nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom conceals wonder; philosophy must transcend custom
rubrics_metrics.description: “Custom doth make dotards of us all. Consider well, thou wilt find that Custom is the greatest of Weavers... Philosophy complains that Custom has hoodwinked us, from the first; that we do everything by Custom, even Believe by it... what is Philosophy throughout but a continual battle against Custom; an ever-renewed effort to transcend the sphere of blind Custom.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom is useful for practical life but numbs the capacity for wonder and critical thought; philosophical effort aims to pierce the enwrapments of custom to recover the miraculous and the original meaning of things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of names to recast reality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Witchcraft, and all manner of Spectre-work, and Demonology, we have now named Madness, and Diseases of the Nerves. ... Ever, as before, does Madness remain a mysterious-terrific ... out of which, indeed, his world of Wisdom has been creatively built together.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renaming or reclassification (e.g., 'witchcraft' → 'madness') changes social perception but does not eliminate the underlying phenomena; beware simplistic re-descriptions that dismiss depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space and Time as enveloping appearances that can be pierced
rubrics_metrics.description: “your two grand fundamental world-enveloping Appearances, SPACE and TIME... lie all-embracing, as the universal canvas... In vain, while here on Earth, shall you endeavor to strip them off; you can, at best, but rend them asunder for moments, and look through.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Space and Time are profound frameworks that shape experience, yet memory, hope, and certain faculties allow temporary transcendence permitting communion with past and future; intellectual and spiritual practice can 'rend' these coverings briefly.
